text: The digestive tract converts feed into the nutrients a chicken's body needs for maintenance, growth, and production such as eggs. Feed is broken down into its basic components: protein, fat, sugar, energy, vitamins. After the beak and mouth, the esophagus carries feed to the crop, which stores swallowed feed and water until it can move on (a long piece of string can cause crop impaction). The proventriculus adds acid and enzymes, starting digestion. The gizzard, unique to birds, is made of two sets of strong muscle that grind feed; backyard chickens swallow small stones that stay in the gizzard to help with grinding — a sharp swallowed object can get stuck there, and a chicken with a damaged gizzard will grow thin and eventually die. The small intestine receives enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver (via the gall bladder) for protein and fat digestion. The ceca, where the small and large intestine join, ferment feed to produce the B vitamins and empty 2–3 times daily, producing mustard-to-dark-brown, smelly droppings. The large intestine absorbs the last of the water. In the cloaca, digestive and urinary wastes mix, which is why droppings are coated with white pasty uric acid. The intestines host beneficial microflora that aid digestion; when other microbes upset this balance, enteritis results, causing diarrhea, increased thirst, dehydration, loss of appetite, weakness, and weight loss or slow growth.
